Here’s a more structured and professional version you can send to Gil that still feels honest, emotional, and real without sounding chaotic or reactive:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="58241"}
Hey Gil, I wanted to be transparent with you about what’s been happening behind the scenes because I’m honestly at a pretty critical point mentally and operationally right now.

My partner has essentially pulled back due to fear, lack of patience, and not fully understanding what it actually takes to build an agency from the ground up. He had a personal real estate deal go south recently, and I think financially and emotionally it’s put him into panic mode. Unfortunately, that panic is now bleeding into the business.

He controls the finances, while I’m the one carrying the day-to-day operations, client fulfillment, sales calls, onboarding, strategy, team management, and growth execution. I’ve been working for free for the last six months trying to build this thing the right way. We launched only a few months ago, and he’s already frustrated we aren’t doing massive numbers yet, despite the fact that we haven’t consistently implemented many of the systems and strategies we’ve been taught.

The biggest issue right now is capacity. Our ads and scheduling consistency are suffering because my calendar is overloaded doing everything else inside the company. I can realistically only take around 6-8 calls a week right now, and with no-shows mixed in, it creates insane pressure on revenue. That pressure then spills into fulfillment because there’s only so much I can physically handle.

I’m trying to solve this immediately by bringing on setters and closers this week so we can increase volume and take pressure off me operationally. I actually believe we’re very close. The team is strong, morale is good overall, and we’re moments away from creating real momentum. But if he fully pulls out financially, we lose the ability to run ads consistently and continue supporting payroll while scaling.

What’s difficult is he isn’t an agency operator. He sees a few months of struggle and thinks the vision is failing, whereas I know enough about this industry to understand traction takes time, especially when you’re building infrastructure while simultaneously learning, refining, hiring, and fulfilling.

On top of that, there’s been volatility emotionally. He’s ghosted for a week at a time, then comes back angry and reactive. Every conversation feels emotionally charged instead of strategic. I recently learned there may also be some substance abuse issues involved, which honestly explains some of the unpredictability.

Another challenge is that he has shiny-object syndrome. We spent heavily upfront trying to look luxury immediately instead of building lean and scaling responsibly as revenue grew. I wanted to fly the plane while building it. He wanted everything polished out of the gate. Now he’s looking at the burn rate and panicking before the systems have had enough time to mature.

The hardest part is I let previous client work fade so I could fully commit to this new venture and vision. I truly believed in what we were building. So now I’m sitting here trying to figure out how to protect clients, staff, fulfillment, and growth while also facing the reality that if he exits, I may have to somehow unwind investments and obligations while still keeping the company alive.

I’m not quitting. I still believe in this deeply. I know the model works. I know the vision is right. But I’d be lying if I said I’m not scared about what happens if the financial side collapses before we fully stabilize.

I just wanted to be honest with you about where things are at.
:::

You can naturally weave that into the message without making it feel overly emotional or unstable. Here’s the revised section added professionally:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="62418"}
Hey Gil, I need to ask that this stays extremely confidential. I do not want to create any additional instability internally, but I’m at a point where I genuinely need high-level CEO guidance and outside perspective from someone who understands what it actually takes to build and scale an agency.

Behind the scenes, I’m dealing with a difficult partner situation that is starting to impact the business operationally and financially. My partner recently experienced a major financial loss personally through a real estate deal, and I believe it has shifted his mindset into fear and panic around the agency.

Compounding that, right after launch in March, I underwent emergency neck surgery related to injuries from an assault by my ex-husband. During that period, while I was temporarily out of commission physically and mentally, several business decisions were made that I may not have fully been part of or aligned with. Since returning, I’ve been trying to stabilize operations, rebuild momentum, and carry the company forward while also recovering personally.

He’s become increasingly frustrated that we are not producing massive revenue only a few months after launch, despite the reality that we are still building infrastructure, refining systems, hiring, and not yet consistently implementing many of the strategies we’ve been taught.

The challenge is that he controls the financial side, while I’m carrying the majority of the operational load: client fulfillment, sales calls, onboarding, strategy, team management, and growth execution. I have not taken a dime from the business in six months and have been working essentially full-time without pay to get this off the ground.

At the moment, capacity has become one of our biggest bottlenecks. My calendar is overloaded handling everything internally, which has created inconsistency in scheduling and ad follow-up. Realistically, I can only manage around 6-8 calls a week right now, and when no-shows happen, it creates significant pressure on revenue generation. That pressure is now spilling into fulfillment because there are simply not enough hours in the day.

I’m actively trying to solve this by bringing on setters and closers this week so we can increase volume, improve consistency, and remove myself as the primary bottleneck. I truly believe we are much closer than it may appear externally. The team itself is strong, morale overall is still positive, and I can see the foundation beginning to take shape.

What worries me is that my partner does not come from the agency world. He expected traction much faster and is struggling to see the long-term vision required to build something sustainable. There has also been increasing emotional volatility, periods of ghosting communication entirely, and reactive conversations centered around fear rather than strategy. It has made leadership and planning very difficult.

Another factor is that we spent aggressively upfront trying to establish a luxury brand presence immediately rather than scaling lean while building revenue. I pushed for a more “fly the plane while building it” approach, but significant money went into branding, assets, tools, and infrastructure early on. Now the burn rate is creating anxiety before the systems have had enough time to fully mature.

The hardest part for me personally is that I let previous client work fade so I could fully commit to this vision. I believed deeply in what we were building and wanted to give it everything I had. Because of that, if he ultimately pulls out financially, I’m left trying to figure out how to continue fulfilling for clients, protect the team, stabilize growth, and potentially navigate dissolving or restructuring obligations tied to the original investment.

I’m not giving up. I still believe in the vision, the offer, and the long-term potential of what we’re building. But I’m carrying a tremendous amount of pressure right now and could really use honest directional input from someone who has experience navigating this stage of business growth and partnership dynamics.
:::
